description: I am coding solo in the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
Astronauts exploring Mars on foot must avoid steep slopes, but slope maps require stereo elevation models (DTMs), which exist for only a small set of sites. Single orbital images cover far more of the planet. A Walk through Jezero Crater asks whether a safe walking route can be planned from images alone.

I trained a U-Net on the Mars 2020 HiRISE orthomosaic of Jezero Crater to label every pixel as safe (under 10°), caution (10–25°) or hazard (25° and up), using slope from the HiRISE elevation model as training labels only. A DoMars16k landform classifier, run on the CTX mosaic, adds cost for dunes and rough terrain. A* search then finds the least-cost walk between any two points.

On a 6 × 6 km region held out from training, the model reached a mean IoU of 0.547, against 0.288 for an image-gradient baseline. Over 200 random 2–6 km walks, the risk-aware routes crossed a true hazard on only 5.5% of routes, versus 21.5% for the plain model and 77.5% with landform data alone, at about 15% extra effort.

An interactive Gradio app lets users pick a start and goal and compare routes with and without an elevation model.
details:
A Walk through Jezero Crater plans safe walking routes for astronauts on Mars. Walkers must avoid steep slopes, and slope normally comes from stereo elevation models (DTMs), which exist for only a few sites. My system predicts slope hazard from a single orbital image, so routes can be planned where no DTM exists.

How it works

  1. A U-Net (ResNet-34 encoder) labels every pixel of the 1 m HiRISE orthomosaic as safe (under 10°), caution (10–25°) or hazard (25° and up). The training labels come from slope computed on the HiRISE DTM. At run time, only the image is needed.
  2. A DoMars16k landform classifier run on the CTX mosaic adds extra cost for dunes, rough terrain and crater fields.
  3. A* search finds the least-cost walk on a 5 m cost grid. A "risk-aware" rule treats any cell with a hazard probability of 10% or more as hazard. That threshold was chosen on a separate validation region before testing.

Results (6 × 6 km test region, kept out of training by a spatial block split)

  • Mean IoU 0.547, against 0.288 for an image-gradient baseline. The model finds 71% of hazard pixels.
  • Over 200 random 2–6 km walks, risk-aware routes crossed a true hazard on 5.5% of routes (95% CI 3.1–9.6%). The plain model did so on 21.5% of routes, and landform data alone on 77.5%. The cost was about 15% more effort than the ideal DTM route.

Impact
Mission planners could scout traverses at any site with orbital images, not just the few sites with elevation models.

Tools
Python, PyTorch, segmentation_models_pytorch, rasterio, scikit-image, NumPy and SciPy. The interactive app is built with Gradio and runs on CPU. In the app, users click a start and goal, switch between DTM and DTM-free mode, and see each route scored on the true terrain.

Factors considered

  • Spatial splits rather than random tiles, so the test region really is unseen.
  • Honest baselines.
  • Confidence intervals on the route results.
  • A known weakness: on west-facing slopes the hazard IoU drops to 0.14, because the model depends on sun angle. The tool is a planning aid, not a guarantee.

Use of AI: Claude (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant for writing and debugging code, research and the slide deck. All figures are rendered by code from real NASA data, not generated by AI.
